vo_text: At the North Pole of Uranus, the seventh planet in orbit around our sun,
markers: *(No overlay in 0–3 s; subject fills centre frame)*

vo_text: what would you see when the sun sinks below the horizon?
A single winter night that lasts twenty-one Earth years.
While Earth spins at a twenty-three point four four degree tilt,
Uranus is tipped at ninety-seven point seven seven degrees, more than four times Earth's tilt,
and nearly at a right angle to its orbit, rolling around the sun on its side like a ball.
markers: Corner disclosure: `INFRARED VIEW` (`25.3–28.8 s`) · Credit: `NASA / ESA / CSA / STScI` (`29.0–31.3 s`)

vo_text: That extreme sideways roll plunges half the planet into twenty-one years of darkness,
markers: Edit label: `21 YEARS OF DARKNESS` (`34.7–38.2 s`)

vo_text: and helps its atmosphere drop to minus two hundred and twenty-four point two degrees Celsius, even colder than farther-out Neptune.
How did an entire giant planet get knocked onto its side? And what did our only spacecraft to visit Uranus find there?
13 March 1781, British astronomer William Herschel searches the night sky for faint stars through a telescope and spots a pale light that moves.
markers: **`WHEN` #1:** `13 MARCH 1781` (`58.1–60.5 s` on timeline) · **`WHO` #1:** `William Herschel` / `(1738–1822) — British astronomer` (`61.0–64.7 s`, `3.7 s` hold) · Credit: `National Portrait Gallery / PD` (`65.2–68.8 s`)

vo_text: It was the first planet found with a telescope and the first new planet discovered since ancient times. Though, at first, Herschel thought it was a comet or a star.
markers: **`FACT` #1:** `FIRST TELESCOPE PLANET` (`70.2–73.9 s`, `3.7 s` hold) · Credit: `Royal Society / PD` (`77.0–80.3 s`)

vo_text: Two years later, in 1783, astronomers accepted this unknown object as a new planet, in part because of observations by German astronomer Johann Elert Bode.
markers: **`WHEN` #2:** `1783` (`81.5–85.0 s` on timeline) · **`WHO` #2:** `Johann Elert Bode` / `(1747–1826) — German astronomer` (`89.5–93.2 s`, `3.7 s` hold)

vo_text: Herschel tried to name his discovery Georgium Sidus after the British monarch. Instead, it was named for Uranus, the Greek god of the sky, as suggested by Johann Bode.
markers: Edit labels: `GEORGIUM SIDUS` (`96.5–99.5 s`) → `URANUS` (`103.6–106.8 s`, one label at a time)

vo_text: With an equatorial diameter of fifty-one thousand, one hundred and eighteen kilometers, Uranus is four times wider than Earth.
If Earth were a nickel, Uranus would be about as big as a softball.
markers: **`SCALE` #2:** `NICKEL VS SOFTBALL` (`118.0–121.8 s`, `3.8 s` hold) · `INFRARED VIEW`

vo_text: From an average distance of two point nine billion kilometers, about 19 astronomical units, or 19 times Earth's distance from the sun,
markers: Edit labels: `2.9 BILLION KM` (`123.5–127.0 s`) → `19 ASTRONOMICAL UNITS` (`127.5–131.3 s`)

vo_text: sunlight takes two hours and 40 minutes to reach Uranus, and one orbit takes about 84 Earth years.
Yet, for nearly two centuries, a deeper secret hid in the dark around it. Why did it take an airplane flying at night to reveal that Uranus was tipped onto its side?
10th March 1977, aboard NASA's Kuiper Airborne Observatory and at the Perth Observatory in Australia,
scientists watch Uranus pass in front of a distant star, SAO one five eight six eight seven. Before and after the planet crosses the star, the starlight blinks off and on.
Uranus, like Saturn, has rings standing nearly upright around a sideways world. Uranus has 13 faint rings,
markers: `INFRARED VIEW` (`177.0–180.5 s`) · **Ch 2 `NUMBER OBJECT` badge:** `13 FAINT RINGS` (`183.7–186.3 s`)

vo_text: nine narrow dark gray inner rings, two more inner rings found in 1986,
and two outer rings discovered by Hubble on 22nd December 2005 and imaged in color in 2006.
The inner one reddish and the outer one blue, like Saturn's E ring.
Orbiting in that tilted plane are 28 known moons, unique in being named for characters from classic English plays and poems.
Why does Uranus spin at a ninety-seven point seven seven-degree tilt, rotating backwards like Venus,
with one day taking about 17 hours, seven hours shorter than Earth's 24-hour day?
markers: **`DATA` #3c (part 2):** `URANUS DAY: 17 HOURS` (`226.5–229.3 s`) → `EARTH DAY: 24 HOURS` (`229.7–233.0 s`)

vo_text: Scientists think this mystery may come from a collision with an Earth-sized object long ago.
markers: Edit label: `EARTH-SIZED IMPACT` (`234.5–238.3 s`, `3.8 s` hold)

vo_text: For nearly a quarter of each 84-year Uranian orbit, the sun shines over one pole, plunging the other half into a 21-year dark winter.
What did our only spacecraft to visit Uranus find when it flew into that world?
If you've enjoyed the ride so far, subscribing is the best way to help Orbit keep going.
24th January 1986, after traveling more than three billion kilometers in nine years, NASA's Voyager 2 makes the first, and so far the only, visit to Uranus.
markers: **`WHEN` #6:** `24 JANUARY 1986` (`266.2–269.8 s` on timeline) · Label: `> 3 BILLION KM · 9 YEARS` (`270.0–273.5 s`)

vo_text: Coming within eighty-one thousand, five hundred kilometers of the cloud tops, Voyager 2 gathers much of its critical information in just six hours, discovering 10 new moons and two new rings.
markers: Label: `81,500 KM ABOVE CLOUDS` (`280.2–283.8 s`) · **`FACT` #3:** `SIX HOURS AT URANUS` (`284.8–288.6 s`, `3.8 s` hold) · Label: `+10 MOONS · +2 RINGS` (`289.1–292.9 s`)

vo_text: What gives Uranus its blue-green color? Its atmosphere is about eighty-two point five percent hydrogen and fifteen point two percent helium,
markers: Edit overlay: `82.5% HYDROGEN · 15.2% HELIUM` (`297.3–303.6 s`, split across `300.5 s` so neither holds `> 4 s`)

vo_text: with two point three percent methane gas that absorbs red sunlight and reflects blue-green light back out.
Inside that atmosphere lies a paradox. Uranus' atmosphere drops to a minimum temperature of 49 Kelvin, minus two hundred and twenty-four point two degrees Celsius.
Why is that a shock? Because it makes Uranus even colder than Neptune in some places,
even though Neptune orbits more than 30 times as far from the Sun as Earth, while Uranus orbits at 19 times Earth's distance.
In 1986, Voyager 2 saw only a few discrete clouds on a calm globe. Case closed? Is Uranus just a sleepy, frozen world where nothing ever changes?
Wrong. Voyager 2 arrived when one pole stared into the sun. 21 years later, as Uranus reached its December 2007 equinox,
when the sun passes over its equator and illuminates the whole planet, the giant woke up.
markers: Edit label: `EQUINOX AWAKENING` (`368.0–371.8 s`, `3.8 s` hold)

vo_text: Through Hubble and ground-based telescopes, astronomers saw dynamic clouds and bright storms erupt across Uranus.
Wind speeds on Uranus reach up to 900 kilometers an hour, 560 miles an hour,
more than twice as fast as Earth's strongest 400-kilometer-an-hour winds, blowing backwards at the equator, then shifting forward closer to the poles.
markers: **`SCALE` #5:** `> 2× EARTH'S 400 KM/H WINDS` (`389.5–393.3 s`) · Label: `RETROGRADE EQUATOR · PROGRADE POLES` (`394.7–398.5 s`)

vo_text: Stranger still is the magnetic field Voyager 2 discovered, stronger than Saturn's, yet completely lopsided.
Magnetic fields normally align with a planet's rotation, but Uranus' magnetic axis is tilted nearly 60 degrees from its spin axis, an offset from the planet's center by one-third of its radius.
Because that lopsided magnet spins sideways every 17 hours,
markers: Edit label: `17-HOUR WOBBLE` (`423.0–426.8 s`, `3.8 s` hold)

vo_text: Uranus' auroras miss the poles, and the magnetosphere tail extending millions of miles behind Uranus twists into a long corkscrew shape.
markers: Edit labels: `AURORAS MISS POLES` (`427.8–431.4 s`) → `CORKSCREW MAGNETOTAIL` (`432.8–436.6 s`)

vo_text: What happens if a spacecraft dives beneath those clouds to land on the ice below?
That brings us to the biggest misconception about Uranus. People hear it is called an ice giant with a minus 224-degree sky and imagine a spacecraft could land on frozen ground.
markers: `INFRARED VIEW` (`445.0–448.5 s`) · Edit label: `ICE GIANT MISCONCEPTION` (`449.0–452.8 s`)

vo_text: As an ice giant, Uranus has no true surface.
Beneath the hydrogen and helium clouds, 80% or more of the planet's mass is a hot, dense fluid of water, methane, and ammonia above a small rocky core.
markers: **`DATA` #6a:** `≥ 80% HOT DENSE FLUID` (`H₂O · CH₄ · NH₃`) → `SMALL ROCKY CORE`

vo_text: Near that core, Uranus heats up to 9,000 degrees Fahrenheit, 4,982 degrees Celsius,
more than 5,000 degrees hotter than its freezing cloud tops.
markers: **`DATA` #6b (part 2) + `SCALE` #6:** `> 5,000 °C HOTTER THAN CLOUDS` (`487.6–491.4 s`, `3.8 s` hold)

vo_text: While a spacecraft has nowhere to land on Uranus, it could not fly through its atmosphere unscathed either. Extreme pressures and temperatures would destroy a metal spacecraft.
markers: Edit overlay: `NO SOLID GROUND` (`494.0–497.8 s`) → `EXTREME PRESSURE & HEAT` (`500.5–504.3 s`)

vo_text: If you cannot land on Uranus, where in this sideways system could you stand on solid ice and look up at those vertical rings?
16th February 1948. At the McDonald Observatory in Western Texas,
markers: **`WHEN` #8:** `16 FEBRUARY 1948` (`514.7–518.1 s` on timeline) · Credit: `Wikimedia / CC BY-SA 3.0` (`518.3–520.6 s`)

vo_text: astronomer Gerard Kuiper discovers Miranda in telescopic photos, the last moon of Uranus found before Voyager 2.
markers: **`WHO` #3:** `Gerard Kuiper` / `(1905–1973) — Dutch-born astronomer` (`521.1–524.8 s`, `3.7 s` hold) · Credit: `Nationaal Archief / CC BY-SA 3.0` (`524.9–525.4 s`)

vo_text: At about 500 kilometers in diameter, Miranda is only one-seventh as large as Earth's moon, a size unlikely to support much tectonic activity.
Yet when Voyager 2 flew past in January 1986, Miranda looked like Frankenstein's monster pieced together from parts that did not merge properly.
markers: Edit label: `PATCHWORK ICE MOON` (`545.5–549.3 s`, `3.8 s` hold)

vo_text: Carving across its surface are giant fault canyons as much as 12 times as deep as Earth's Grand Canyon.
Because of Miranda's low gravity and towering cliffs, a rock dropped off the highest cliff would take 10 minutes to reach the foot of the cliff.
On 19th of April 2022, the Planetary Science Decadal Survey for 2023 to 2032 outlined a new Uranus mission as a highest priority objective,
markers: **`WHEN` #9:** `19 APRIL 2022 · 2023–2032` (`570.8–574.6 s` on timeline) · Label: `TOP PRIORITY MISSION` (`577.5–581.3 s`)

vo_text: and in October 2024, Hubble and New Horizons simultaneously observed Uranus from two viewpoints.
Uranus is a sideways giant of 21-year winters, corkscrew magnetism, and 10-minute cliffs.
